items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. floods force evacuations, shelter orders as roads close
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

The researchers say these regions help regulate Earth’s energy, water and carbon cycles, and their decline increases the risks of sea-level rise, ecosystem damage and flooding. The team assessed four indicators against conditions over the past 11,700 years, when a relatively stable climate allowed human civilizations to develop. The researchers say the findings support urgent cuts to greenhouse-gas emissions and call for limits on black carbon and local disturbances such as industrial expansion. The authors released the paper during the COP31 climate conference and urged policymakers to use the proposed boundaries in climate planning.

items.title: [japantimes.co.jp] Climate change intensified Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade, study finds
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A World Weather Attribution study published Friday found that a strong El Niño drove Indonesia’s severe rainfall shortfall this year, while human-caused climate change made temperatures during the August-to-October fire season about 1.6 degrees Celsius higher. Researchers said warming made hot, dry fire conditions about three times more likely, while El Niño cut seasonal rainfall by roughly half. Decades of deforestation and peatland drainage also left the landscape more vulnerable to ignition. The fires have spread hazardous haze across Indonesia and neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitoring platform, estimated that fires affected 2.88 million hectares from January through October. The Indonesian government had not confirmed that total or issued its own estimate. Researchers called for peatland restoration, stronger land protections and reduced fossil-fuel emissions. Fires were still burning, with smoke detected in eastern Kalimantan on Nov. 12.

items.title: [tsln.com] Cattle specialists urge targeted winter feeding to manage costs
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

items.title: [spravy.stvr.sk] AI data-center developers plan 181 GW of fossil-fuel power plants
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Developers are proposing 181 gigawatts of fossil-fuel power plants beside planned AI data centers in the United States, Britain and continental Europe to avoid lengthy grid-connection delays, according to research firm BloombergNEF. If built, about 90% of the plants would be in the United States and produce an estimated 345 million metric tons of carbon-dioxide equivalent annually. BloombergNEF forecasts that AI data-center electricity demand will reach 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, nearly four times current levels and about 7% of global electricity use. Data-center electricity demand is growing faster than grid capacity, while households are covering part of the infrastructure costs. In the United States, data-center electricity demand has risen 19% a year since 2020, while grid capacity has expanded 2% annually. A separate estimate found that data centers covered only 38% of the $8.25 billion in grid costs associated with their growth in 2025, leaving residents to pay most of the remainder.

items.title: [scimex.org] Astronomers trace eight-minute radio pulses to white dwarf and Sun-like star
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Astronomers have traced repeating radio pulses from the system GPM J071507−114153 to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star—the first known long-period radio transient with this type of stellar pairing. The pulses recur every 7.9 minutes but appear only during a roughly six-hour window in each 32-hour orbit. The system lies more than 5,000 light-years away. Researchers discovered the system using Australia’s Murchison Widefield Array, pinpointed it with South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope and used the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to identify the companion as a G-type star. Measurements of the orbit and the companion’s slight movement indicate that the pulsing object has about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, making it too light to be a neutron star. The study was published in Nature Astronomy on Nov. 12, 2026.

The Swedish Board of Agriculture forecast a strong 2025 grain harvest of 5.9 million tonnes in mid-August, after farm cooperative Lantmännen projected 5.5 million tonnes in early July. The larger crop followed two weak growing seasons, but low grain prices and high input costs continued to weigh on arable farmers’ profitability, Lantmännen’s grain chief Per Germundsson said. Farmers were also considering more on-farm storage after delivery bottlenecks during the busy harvest.

Canada’s federal government will not appeal an Alberta Court of Appeal ruling that parts of the Impact Assessment Act exceed federal authority and says it will amend the law to address the ruling. Ottawa has not announced the details or timing of the amendments. They are expected to be developed alongside Bill C-39, now before Parliament, which would shorten project reviews and shift assessments of pipelines, power lines and some nuclear and uranium projects to specialist regulators.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [blog.ovhcloud.com] PHP hosting provider backports fixes across six million sites as patching lags
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Hosting provider OVHcloud says it deployed official fixes or its own backports across all 15 PHP versions on its shared-hosting platform, covering more than 6 million websites on about 5,000 servers. The fixes address two PHP flaws collectively known as PHP2Shell that can let attackers run commands on vulnerable servers without credentials. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has confirmed active exploitation and set an Oct. 29 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address the flaws. Censys’ tracker showed more than 10 million services patched since Oct. 21, while a scan found more than 4 million services in Germany still reporting vulnerable PHP version numbers. The scanner cautions that backported fixes may not appear in those version strings. OVHcloud says it wrote fixes for PHP 5.3 through 7.3, versions the PHP project no longer maintains. Researchers documented 35 shell executions on three deliberately vulnerable honeypots, but the test used a favorable single-worker setup. CISA has not named affected organizations or described the evidence behind its listing, and the designation does not establish the scale of successful compromises in production. Some earlier claims of successful exploitation were withdrawn or qualified after investigators found scanning or could not confirm PHP2Shell as the entry point.

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.content_html:

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.title: [addisstandard.com] Amnesty says South Sudan, UN failed to prevent Abiemnom massacre
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Amnesty International said South Sudanese authorities and the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) failed to act on advance warnings before armed men attacked Abiemnom on March 1, killing at least 213 people. In a report released Nov. 12, the rights group said 1,000 to 1,500 men from Mayom County carried out a four-hour assault, burning homes and attacking part of the local hospital. The death toll reported by South Sudanese authorities included 130 residents, 76 security personnel and seven foreign nationals. Amnesty said authorities and UNMISS had received warnings of a possible attack about two weeks earlier, and that around 1,000 residents sought refuge at a UNMISS base in the 48 hours before the assault. items._excerpt: Amnesty International said South Sudanese authorities and the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) failed to act on advance warnings before armed men attacked Abiemnom on March 1, killing at least 213 people. In a report released Nov. 12, the rights group said 1,000 to 1,500 men from Mayom County carried out a four-hour assault, burning homes and attacking part of the local hospital. The death toll reported by South Sudanese authorities included 130 residents, 76 security personnel and seven foreign nationals (addisstandard.com, eastleighvoice.co.ke, deccanchronicle.com). Amnesty said authorities and UNMISS had received warnings of a possible attack about two weeks earlier, and that around 1,000 residents sought refuge at a UNMISS base in the 48 hours before the assault. UNMISS said it focused its limited capacity on people sheltering at its base and sent 40 additional police personnel after the attack (africanews.com, eastleighvoice.co.ke, deccanchronicle.com). Evidence reviewed: Amnesty said it interviewed 82 people, including 76 survivors and witnesses, and examined satellite imagery, photographs and videos; the imagery showed more than 230 structures burned (eastleighvoice.co.ke, addisstandard.com). Killings near the UN base: Amnesty documented seven killings near the UNMISS base, where residents had fled seeking protection (addisstandard.com, africanews.com). UN staffing: The U.N. Security Council renewed UNMISS’s mandate in April while lowering its authorized troop ceiling from 17,000 to 12,000 (deccanchronicle.com). Alleged trigger: Amnesty said unresolved killings of young men from Mayom County may have triggered the assault, against a backdrop of earlier retaliatory violence (eastleighvoice.co.ke, deccanchronicle.com).

items.title: [3dprinting.com] 3D-printed tungsten tiles withstand 74 plasma discharges in fusion test
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.

items.title: [wsws.org] Youth protests over costs spread across Europe as German rallies turn violent
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Youth-led demonstrations over living costs, education, housing and public services drew crowds across Europe on Saturday, with violence breaking out after rallies in several German cities. Organizers of Germany’s “Gen Z regelt” movement estimated 120,000 participants across more than 30 cities. Most marches were peaceful, but looting, fires and clashes with police followed rallies in Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg. In Frankfurt, authorities reported at least 54 arrests and more than 100 injured police officers. France’s third consecutive weekend of protests drew an estimated 320,000 people, including 70,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry; police made 779 arrests nationwide. Demonstrations also took place in Portugal, where police cleared a tent camp in Lisbon after a housing protest, and in Zurich, where police said rioters set vehicles and barricades alight. Participants in Germany also opposed spending cuts and plans to revive compulsory military service. Organizers rejected violence, while German officials blamed extremist groups and called for penalties against those involved. Gen Z regelt has called for another demonstration on Nov. 14; a separate Europe-wide protest is planned for Nov. 20.
